implementation_notes: Rust replaces Dispose with the Drop trait: when a value is no longer needed - most commonly at end of scope - its destructor runs, and the compiler-generated 'drop glue' recursively calls the destructors of all fields, so an owner releases everything it owns with no explicit call and no way to forget. Order is guaranteed (struct fields in declaration order, local variables in reverse declaration order) and local values are dropped while unwinding from a panic. Drop::drop cannot be called directly - mem::drop(value) is the explicit early release, ManuallyDrop opts out for handover/FFI cases - and a type cannot be both Copy and Drop, so ownership edges stay unambiguous; borrowed values are plain references and are never dropped, which gives the borrowed-resource exclusion for free. Keep an explicit close()-style API only when release must report errors or return the resource to a pool.
pitfalls: A panic inside Drop::drop while already unwinding aborts the process (double panic); cleanup must be best-effort and not panic.
Values that never drop - mem::forget, Rc cycles, ManuallyDrop, or a process that exits - never run the destructor, so the safety net is gone on exactly those paths.
In async code, dropping a future cancels it: resources held across an await point must be released by the future's Drop or wrapped in a guard, and spawned tasks own their values.
